items.intro: As part of a university project, you have agreed to take part in a short research interview about work-life balance. Answer each question in the time allowed.

questions.question: Do you feel that you currently have a good balance between your work and personal life? Give details to explain your answer.
questions.reference_answer: I think I have a fairly good balance right now because I set clear limits on when I study and when I rest. On weekdays I finish my most important tasks first, and in the evening I try to exercise or talk with friends. This keeps me from feeling that work takes over my whole life.

questions.question: Can you describe some strategies you use or want to use to maintain a balanced lifestyle?
questions.reference_answer: One strategy I use is planning my week in advance. I write down deadlines, but I also schedule time for sleep, exercise, and family. I try not to check messages late at night because that makes it harder to relax.

questions.question: Tell me about a time when you felt overwhelmed by work or personal responsibilities. How did you handle the situation?
questions.reference_answer: Last semester I felt overwhelmed when two exams and a group project were due in the same week. I handled it by making a list, dividing the work into smaller tasks, and asking my group members to meet earlier. That helped me feel more in control.

questions.question: Some people believe that employers should offer more flexible working arrangements to help employees better achieve a healthy work-life balance. Do you agree or disagree with this idea? Why?
questions.reference_answer: I agree that employers should offer flexible working arrangements. Flexible hours or remote work can reduce stress and help people manage family responsibilities. Of course, employees still need to finish their work, but flexibility often helps them become more focused and loyal.

items.intro: A researcher is studying people's views on art and self-expression. Answer the interviewer's questions and say as much as you can in the time allowed.

questions.question: Do you engage in any artistic activities, such as painting or playing music, regularly? If so, what do you do? If not, which artistic activity would you like to try if you had the chance?
questions.reference_answer: I do not practice an artistic activity regularly, but I would like to learn digital illustration. I often need to explain ideas visually for school projects, and drawing would help me turn those ideas into clear images. I would begin with simple tools on a tablet and practice basic shapes, color, and composition for about twenty minutes a day. Later, I would try designing posters for campus events. This activity appeals to me because it combines creativity with practical communication. It would also give me a relaxing break from academic work while still producing something useful that I could improve over time.

questions.question: What form of art or music do you enjoy most, and how do you typically experience it through creation or appreciation?
questions.reference_answer: I enjoy photography most, especially photographs of ordinary city life. I usually experience it through appreciation rather than creation. I follow several documentary photographers online and pay attention to how they use light, distance, and timing to make a familiar street look meaningful. When I visit a museum, I also spend time reading the captions because the social context often changes how I understand an image. Although I take pictures with my phone, I do not consider them serious work yet. Still, studying strong photographs has made me more observant and has taught me that visual details can tell a complex story without many words.

questions.question: Would you prefer sharing your work publicly or keeping it private? What influences your decision?
questions.reference_answer: I would prefer to share selected work publicly, but not everything I create. Public sharing can be useful because feedback shows me what viewers understand and where my message is unclear. For example, if I designed a poster, comments from classmates could help me improve the layout or wording. However, early drafts are often experimental, and publishing them too soon might make me focus on approval instead of learning. Therefore, I would keep rough work private, revise it carefully, and share only pieces that represent my real intention. My decision depends mainly on whether feedback would support the project rather than distract me from developing it.

questions.question: Art and music can be powerful ways to communicate emotions and ideas that are difficult to express with words. Do you agree or disagree? Why?
questions.reference_answer: I agree because art and music can express emotional experiences that ordinary explanations often flatten. A melody can create tension, calm, or hope before a listener has analyzed any words, and an image can show several feelings at once. For example, a photograph of an empty classroom after graduation may communicate pride, loss, and change more effectively than a list of statements. This does not mean words are unimportant. Instead, artistic forms add tone, rhythm, and perspective to the message. They allow people from different backgrounds to respond emotionally even when they do not share the same language or personal history.

items.intro: As part of a university research project, you have agreed to take part in a short interview about personal finances. A graduate student conducting the research will ask you some questions.

questions.question: Thanks in advance for your time today. I'd like to ask you about your personal finance habits. To start off, do you typically keep a budget for your expenses, or do you manage them informally?
questions.reference_answer: I usually keep a simple monthly budget because it helps me see where my money is going. At the beginning of each month, I list fixed expenses such as rent, transportation, and phone service. Then I set limits for food, entertainment, and online shopping. I do not record every small purchase immediately, but I check my bank app every few days and update the totals. This system is flexible enough for real life, yet it still keeps me from spending carelessly. If an unexpected expense appears, I reduce my entertainment budget instead of using savings. For me, a basic written plan works better than managing everything informally because it makes my priorities visible.

questions.question: Everyone has different spending habits. Who or what would you say most influences the way you make money-related choices: your family, your friends, or your own experience? Why?
questions.reference_answer: My own experience influences my money-related choices the most, although my family gave me a useful foundation. When I first started living away from home, I underestimated how quickly small purchases could add up. I spent too much on delivery food and had very little left at the end of the month. After that, I began comparing prices, planning meals, and waiting before buying things I did not truly need. Friends sometimes recommend products, but I do not automatically follow them because our budgets and priorities are different. Personal experience has taught me to consider long-term value, not just the excitement of buying something new, so it now guides most of my decisions.

questions.question: If you were to receive extra money, such as a gift, how would you decide what to do with it? For instance, would you spend it or save it, and why?
questions.reference_answer: If I received extra money as a gift, I would divide it instead of spending or saving all of it. I would put most of the money, perhaps seventy percent, into savings for emergencies or future tuition. Saving the larger share would make the gift useful long after I received it. I would use the remaining amount for one meaningful purchase or experience, such as a short trip with friends or a useful piece of equipment. That would let me enjoy the gift without feeling irresponsible. Before deciding, I would also check whether I had any urgent bills. This balanced approach fits me because it combines security with a small, memorable reward.

questions.question: Some experts believe that personal finance should be something that schools teach to prepare young people for future money management. Do you agree? How could such classes affect students?
questions.reference_answer: Yes, I think schools should teach personal finance because students often face important money decisions before they have much practical experience. A useful course could explain budgeting, bank accounts, interest, credit cards, taxes, and the risks of borrowing. For example, a student who understands compound interest is less likely to treat a credit-card limit as free money. The class should include realistic activities, such as planning a monthly budget or comparing loan offers, rather than only definitions. It would not guarantee that every student makes perfect choices, but it would give them a common set of tools. That preparation could reduce avoidable debt and help young adults feel more confident when they begin working or living independently.

items.intro: You have agreed to answer questions about commuting and travel routines. An interviewer will ask you some questions.

questions.question: What kinds of places do you usually go to during the week, and how do you get there?
questions.reference_answer: During the week, I usually go to campus, the public library, a gym, and a supermarket near my apartment. I take the bus to campus because it is several kilometers away, but I walk to the library and supermarket when the weather is good. For the gym, I normally ride my bicycle because there is a safe bike lane. I plan each trip around my class schedule, so I can combine errands instead of traveling back and forth. This routine saves money, gives me some exercise, and makes my weekdays feel organized rather than rushed.

questions.question: Can you describe how someone in your family or a friend usually travels to work or school? How much time does it take, and what transportation does the person use?
questions.reference_answer: My older sister travels to work by subway on most weekdays. She walks about ten minutes from her apartment to the station, rides the train for roughly thirty minutes, and then walks another five minutes to her office. The whole trip takes around forty-five minutes. She prefers the subway because traffic in her city is unpredictable, while the trains usually arrive on time. During the ride, she reads the news or reviews her schedule for the day. If she has to stay late at work, she sometimes takes a taxi home, but that is much more expensive.

questions.question: Some people believe that living close to work or school improves quality of life, while others think location does not matter much. What do you think and why?
questions.reference_answer: I believe living close to work or school clearly improves quality of life. A shorter commute gives people more time for sleep, exercise, family, and personal interests. It also reduces the stress of traffic delays or crowded public transportation. One of my friends moved from the suburbs to an apartment near our campus. Before moving, she spent almost two hours commuting each day and often missed morning activities. Now she can walk to class in fifteen minutes, attends study groups regularly, and feels less tired. Location is not the only factor in happiness, but it strongly shapes a person's daily routine and energy.

questions.question: Some people believe that employers should reimburse employees for their commuting costs, while others think that employees should pay for their own travel to work. Which view do you agree with and why?
questions.reference_answer: I think employers should reimburse at least part of employees' commuting costs when regular office attendance is required. Transportation is a necessary expense connected directly to the job, especially in cities where housing near business districts is unaffordable. A company could provide a public transit pass or a fixed monthly allowance instead of paying every possible expense. This approach would control costs while helping workers who travel long distances. It could also encourage employees to use buses and trains, which reduces traffic and pollution. Employees would still choose where to live, but employers would share a reasonable portion of the cost of reaching the workplace.

questions.question: How often do you use public transportation like buses or trains? Give details to explain your answer.
questions.reference_answer: I use public transportation several times a week, mostly buses and the subway. I take them when I go to school or meet friends because they are cheaper than taking a taxi and I do not need to worry about parking. For example, when I have classes downtown, the subway is usually faster than driving during rush hour. I also like that I can read or review notes while I travel. It is not perfect, but it is practical for my daily routine.

questions.question: Can you describe any benefits or disadvantages you might experience from using public transportation?
questions.reference_answer: One benefit is that public transportation saves money and can be less stressful than driving in traffic. It also helps reduce pollution because many people share the same vehicle instead of using separate cars. The main disadvantage is reliability. Buses or trains can be delayed, and during rush hour they may be crowded and uncomfortable. For instance, if a bus arrives late before an exam, I may feel anxious. So I like public transportation, but I usually leave extra time.

questions.question: Would you consider moving in order to have better public transportation? Why or why not?
questions.reference_answer: Yes, I would consider moving if the new place had much better public transportation. A reliable subway or bus system would save time every day and make it easier to get to school, work, and social activities without depending on a car. For example, living near a direct train line could reduce a one-hour commute to thirty minutes. I would still consider rent and safety, but transportation would be an important reason to move.

questions.question: Some people believe that cities should invest more in public transportation to fight congestion, commuting time, and pollution. Do you agree or disagree with this idea? Why?
questions.reference_answer: I agree that cities should invest more in public transportation. Better buses and trains can reduce the number of cars on the road, which lowers traffic congestion and air pollution. It also helps students, workers, and older people travel more easily. For example, if buses arrive frequently and connect to major neighborhoods, fewer people need to drive downtown. Although building transportation systems costs money, the long-term benefits for the city are worth it.

items.intro: You have agreed to participate in a research study about people's experiences with recycling and waste management. You will have a short online interview with a researcher.

questions.question: Do you regularly recycle items such as paper, plastic, and glass? Why or why not?
questions.reference_answer: Yes, I regularly recycle paper, plastic, glass, and metal when suitable collection bins are available. I do it because recycling keeps reusable materials out of landfills and reduces the need to extract new resources. I also find that the habit becomes easy once containers are placed in convenient locations. At home, I keep a small box for paper and a separate bin for bottles and cans, so sorting does not take much time. I still check local rules because not every type of plastic is accepted. Recycling is not a complete solution to waste, but it is a practical daily action that most people can maintain.

questions.question: Can you describe the recycling practices in your household or community?
questions.reference_answer: In my household, we separate paper, plastic containers, glass bottles, and ordinary trash. We rinse containers and place the recycling in labeled bins near the kitchen, which makes the system simple for everyone. Our community collects these materials once a week and provides a separate drop-off point for electronics and batteries. The local website also explains which items are accepted. This clear guidance is important because people sometimes place food waste or plastic bags in the wrong bin. Community volunteers occasionally share reminders and organize collection days. These practices work best when the rules are visible, collection is reliable, and residents can ask questions easily.

questions.question: What challenges or difficulties do you face when trying to recycle? And how do you overcome them?
questions.reference_answer: The biggest challenge is uncertainty about what can actually be recycled. Packaging often combines paper, plastic, and metal, and local programs do not accept every material. Limited storage can also be a problem, especially when collection occurs only once a week. I overcome these difficulties by checking the recycling symbol and the local collection website before sorting unfamiliar items. I flatten boxes to save space and keep batteries or electronics in a separate container until I can take them to a drop-off site. When an item is not recyclable, I try to reduce waste by reusing it or choosing products with simpler packaging the next time I shop.

questions.question: Some people believe that effective recycling programs are crucial for reducing pollution and conserving natural resources and therefore should be mandatory. Do you agree or disagree with this belief? Why or why not?
questions.reference_answer: I agree that basic recycling programs should be mandatory, provided that communities make participation practical and affordable. Pollution and resource use affect everyone, so a voluntary system often leaves too many recyclable materials in landfills. A mandatory program could require households and businesses to separate common items such as paper, glass, metal, and accepted plastics. However, rules alone are not enough. Local governments should provide clearly labeled bins, frequent collection, and simple instructions in several languages. They should also begin with education before issuing penalties. With convenient services and reasonable standards, a mandatory program can create consistent habits, reduce contamination, and conserve resources without placing an unfair burden on residents.
